interactions.label: Which mechanism maintains corneal transparency by causing scattered light waves

params.question: Which mechanism maintains corneal transparency by causing scattered light waves to cancel each other out?

answers.text: Anti-angiogenic factors at the limbus preventing vessel ingrowth

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Anti-angiogenic factors maintain avascularity, a separate transparency mechanism. Avascularity prevents light-scattering blood vessels from entering the cornea but does not involve destructive interference.

answers.text: Regular spacing of Type I collagen fibrils in the stroma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! The precisely spaced Type I collagen fibrils form the Maurice lattice. This regular arrangement causes destructive interference — scattered light waves cancel each other out, allowing the cornea to remain transparent.
The endothelial pump removes water from the stroma to prevent oedema, which is the third transparency mechanism. It does not involve destructive interference of light.

answers.text: Continuous renewal of the epithelium by limbal stem cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Limbal stem cells replenish the epithelium, maintaining its integrity. This is important for corneal health but is not one of the three transparency mechanisms described.

overallFeedback.feedback: The Maurice lattice of regularly spaced Type I collagen fibrils causes destructive interference, where scattered light waves cancel each other out. This is one of three corneal transparency mechanisms, alongside avascularity and the endothelial pump.

Correct! The Maurice lattice — regularly spaced Type I collagen fibrils — produces destructive interference of scattered light, one of three mechanisms alongside avascularity and endothelial pump dehydration.

params.question: A child presents with bilateral corneal enlargement exceeding 13 mm. Which finding confirms buphthalmos rather than megalocornea?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both megalocornea and buphthalmos can have a corneal diameter above 13 mm. Diameter alone cannot distinguish the two conditions.
Both conditions can present bilaterally. Symmetry of enlargement does not favour one diagnosis over the other.

Correct! Haab's striae are horizontal tears in Descemet's membrane caused by the globe stretching under raised intraocular pressure — pathognomonic of buphthalmos. Megalocornea has a clear cornea and normal pressure.

answers.text: Clear cornea with a normal anterior segment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A clear cornea with normal anterior segment favours megalocornea, the benign X-linked condition. Buphthalmos presents with a cloudy cornea and requires urgent surgical intervention.

overallFeedback.feedback: Buphthalmos is distinguished from megalocornea by raised intraocular pressure, a cloudy cornea, and Haab's striae — horizontal tears in Descemet's membrane from globe stretching. Megalocornea has a clear cornea and normal pressure. Always measure IOP in a child with a large cornea.

Correct! Haab's striae with raised intraocular pressure confirm buphthalmos — congenital glaucoma requiring urgent goniotomy or trabeculotomy. Always measure eye pressure before calling any large cornea benign.

params.question: A patient has a Schirmer's test wetting of 14 mm but a tear film break-up time of 6 seconds. Which type of dry eye does this indicate?

answers.text: Aqueous-deficient dry eye from lacrimal gland failure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Aqueous-deficient dry eye would show reduced Schirmer's wetting (below 10 mm). This patient's Schirmer's test is normal at 14 mm, indicating adequate lacrimal secretion.

answers.text: Evaporative dry eye from meibomian gland dysfunction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Normal aqueous output (Schirmer's 14 mm) with a short break-up time (6 seconds, under 10) indicates an unstable tear film despite adequate volume — the hallmark of evaporative dry eye, most commonly from meibomian gland dysfunction.

answers.text: Mucin-deficient dry eye from goblet cell destruction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While mucin deficiency can destabilise the tear film, the two-test classification distinguishes aqueous-deficient from evaporative dry eye. Normal Schirmer's with short TBUT specifically points to the evaporative type.
Combined dry eye would show both reduced Schirmer's wetting (below 10 mm) and a short break-up time. This patient's Schirmer's test is normal, ruling out aqueous deficiency.

overallFeedback.feedback: Schirmer's test measures aqueous tear production (abnormal <10 mm), while tear film break-up time measures film stability (abnormal <10 seconds). Normal production + unstable film = evaporative dry eye, usually from meibomian gland dysfunction.

Correct! Normal Schirmer's (≥10 mm) with a short break-up time (<10 s) indicates evaporative dry eye — the tear film is unstable despite adequate aqueous volume. Meibomian gland dysfunction is the commonest cause overall.

params.question: A patient with progressive keratoconus has an intact endothelium confirmed on specular microscopy. Which keratoplasty is most appropriate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Penetrating keratoplasty replaces all corneal layers and carries the highest rejection risk. It is the last resort, reserved for disease spanning all layers — not appropriate when the endothelium is healthy.

Correct! DALK replaces only the anterior layers while preserving the patient's own healthy endothelium. This eliminates the risk of endothelial rejection and avoids the need for lifelong immunosuppression.
DSEK selectively replaces the endothelium. It is indicated for endothelial failure (e.g., Fuchs' dystrophy or pseudophakic bullous keratopathy), not for anterior stromal disease like keratoconus.
Like DSEK, DMEK targets the endothelium and Descemet's membrane. It is the procedure of choice for isolated endothelial disease, not for the anterior stromal thinning of keratoconus.

overallFeedback.feedback: In keratoconus with an intact endothelium, DALK is preferred — it replaces only the anterior layers, sparing the patient's healthy endothelium. DSEK and DMEK target endothelial disease; penetrating keratoplasty is reserved for full-thickness involvement.
Correct! DALK preserves the patient's own endothelium, eliminating endothelial rejection risk. The guiding principle: choose the keratoplasty type based on which layer is diseased.

interactions.label: Topical steroids alone can safely be used to treat a dendritic corneal ulcer.

params.question: Topical steroids alone can safely be used to treat a dendritic corneal ulcer.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Steroids must never be used alone in active herpes simplex epithelial keratitis. Without antiviral cover (topical aciclovir), steroids suppress the immune response, allowing the virus to spread from a dendritic pattern to a geographic ulcer — a potentially blinding complication.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Well reasoned! Topical steroids without antiviral cover in a dendritic ulcer (herpes simplex keratitis) suppress the local immune response, allowing unchecked viral replication. This converts the dendritic ulcer into a larger, more destructive geographic ulcer — the most dangerous error in corneal ulcer management.
